author: George Eliot
auditor_notes: Lessons audited across Edexcel (7 lessons) and Eduqas (8 lessons). Primary sources: novel text (Project Gutenberg PG 550), Wikipedia, SparkNotes, LitCharts, CliffsNotes, Shmoop, GradeSaver, eNotes. Factual errors flagged only; interpretation not flagged. 21 chapters in 2 parts + Conclusion confirmed. Key verifiable facts used: Dunsey entered cottage when Silas was absent (gone for a piece of twine), not during a cataleptic fit; Eppie's arrival is the cataleptic-fit scene; the 'debts we can't pay' line is Godfrey's in Ch.20; Marley's chain is from A Christmas Carol not Silas Marner; opening epigraph is Wordsworth's 'Michael', not the 'city of destruction' passage.

issues.location: Edexcel L3 body text: 'Dunstan Cass (known as Dunsey) discovers Silas's cottage empty during one of his cataleptic fits and steals the entire hoard'; Eduqas L3 body text: 'Dunsey finds Silas's cottage empty and steals the money instead'; Eduqas L3 flashcard: 'Q: What type of fit is Silas experiencing when the theft happens? A: A cataleptic fit — a trance-like seizure'; Eduqas L3 flashcard: 'Q: How does Dunstan Cass enter Silas's cottage? A: The door is left open while Silas is having a cataleptic fit.'
issues.claim: Dunsey steals Silas's gold while Silas is having a cataleptic fit, with the door left open because of that fit.
issues.correct_fact: In Chapter 4, Silas is simply not at home when Dunsey steals the gold — he had gone out to fetch a piece of twine needed for the next day's work. The cottage door was unlocked because Silas had never needed to lock it, not because he was in a trance. Dunsey knocks, gets no answer, finds the door unlocked, and lets himself in to an empty cottage. The cataleptic fit that allows Eppie to enter through an open door occurs separately, on New Year's Eve (Chapter 12), not during the theft. The two events are distinct and must not be conflated.
issues.source: Silas Marner Ch.4: Dunsey finds cottage empty, Silas had gone out for twine; SparkNotes Ch.3-4 summary; LitCharts Ch.4 summary; CliffsNotes Ch.3-4 summary; GradeSaver Part 1 Ch.3-5 summary.

issues.location: Eduqas L5 body text: 'Godfrey is devastated by Eppie's rejection. Nancy tells him: "There's debts we can't pay like money debts, by paying extra for the years that have slipped by."'; Eduqas L5 practice question mark scheme: 'Nancy says: "There's debts we can't pay like money debts, by paying extra for the years that have slipped by."'; Eduqas L5 flashcard: 'Q: Which Nancy line states the novel's moral about debts? A: "There's debts we can't pay like money debts, by paying extra for the years that have slipped by."'
issues.claim: Nancy Lammeter says 'There's debts we can't pay like money debts, by paying extra for the years that have slipped by.'
issues.correct_fact: This line is spoken by Godfrey Cass, not Nancy Lammeter. In Chapter 20, after Eppie refuses to go with them, Godfrey says 'there's debts we can't pay like money debts, by paying extra for the years that have slipped by.' It is Godfrey's self-condemning reflection on his own moral failure, not Nancy's judgement of him. Nancy's response in this scene is one of acceptance and mild reproof; she does not deliver this moral observation. Misattributing the line to Nancy inverts who is being blamed and who is acknowledging guilt.
issues.source: Silas Marner Ch.20 (American Literature online text; Wikisource 1878 edition; CliffsNotes Ch.20 analysis; GradeSaver Ch.18-20 summary; SparkNotes Ch.19-21 summary).

issues.location: Eduqas L8 body text exam technique section: 'Three key techniques: (1) Symbolism — gold/Eppie parallel, stone-pit, Marley's chain.'
issues.claim: Marley's chain is a key technique or symbol in Silas Marner.
issues.correct_fact: Marley's chain is a symbol from A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens, not from Silas Marner by George Eliot. Jacob Marley's ghost appears dragging chains of cash-boxes and ledgers in Dickens's novella. There is no character named Marley and no chain motif of that description in Silas Marner. The lesson appears to have cross-contaminated a symbol from a different GCSE text. The correct central symbols in Silas Marner are the gold coins, Eppie's golden curls, the hearth, the stone-pit, and the loom.
issues.source: Silas Marner (George Eliot, 1861) — no Marley or chain-of-cash-boxes motif. A Christmas Carol (Charles Dickens, 1843) — Marley's chain is described in Stave 1.

issues.location: Edexcel L2 body text: 'Eliot's narrator describes this process using the novel's opening quotation: "In old days there were angels who came and took men by the hand and led them away from the city of destruction. We see no white-winged angels now."'; Eduqas L6 practice question: 'Read the following extract about Silas: "In old days there were angels who came and took men by the hand and led them away from the city of destruction. We see no white-winged angels now. But yet men are led away from threatening destruction..."'
issues.claim: The 'In old days there were angels' passage is described as the novel's 'opening quotation.'
issues.correct_fact: The novel's opening epigraph (the quotation printed before Chapter 1) is taken from Wordsworth's poem 'Michael': 'A child, more than all other gifts / That earth can offer to declining man, / Brings hope with it, and forward-looking thoughts.' The 'angels / city of destruction' passage appears in the body of the novel at Chapter 14 as part of the narrator's reflection on Silas's redemption through Eppie. Calling it the 'opening quotation' is factually inaccurate; it is an interior narrator passage, not the epigraph.
issues.source: Silas Marner (Project Gutenberg PG 550): epigraph is Wordsworth 'Michael'; 'angels' passage is in Ch.14. Shmoop: 'What's Up With the Epigraph?' confirming Wordsworth source. LitCharts Ch.14 analysis.

issues.location: Edexcel L2 body text: 'William Dane plants Silas's knife at the scene to frame him.' Edexcel L2 flashcard: 'Q: Who frames Silas for theft at Lantern Yard? A: William Dane, who plants Silas's knife at the scene after stealing the deacon's money.'
issues.claim: William Dane frames Silas solely by planting his knife at the scene of the theft.
issues.correct_fact: Eliot presents two pieces of incriminating evidence in Chapter 1: (1) Silas's pocket-knife is found at the deacon's bureau (where the money was kept), suggesting William placed it there; (2) the empty money-bag is discovered in Silas's own room during the subsequent search, which William Dane himself conducts. Silas later realises he had lent the knife to William and never got it back. Describing the framing as solely a knife plant omits the planted money-bag found in Silas's dwelling, which is the more damning piece of evidence and the one that seals his conviction. Both details together constitute the frame-up.
issues.source: Silas Marner Ch.1: knife found at bureau, bag found in Silas's room; SparkNotes Ch.1-2 summary; LitCharts Ch.1 analysis; GradeSaver Ch.1-2 summary; eNotes William Dane character analysis.
